e.meaning: of Christ (short for Kristopher, Kristian or Kristin)
e.etymology: A K spelling of Chris, short for Kristopher, Kristian, Kristin, Kristina and their Ch- twins, all built on Greek Khristos, the anointed one.
namesakes: Kris Jenner (Kardashian family matriarch and manager)

assoc.t: Kris Kringle, another name for Santa Claus
Kris Jenner, Kardashian family matriarch

e.etymology: A spelling of Kelsey shaped by Chelsea. Kelsey is an English surname, from villages in Lincolnshire or from the Old English personal name Ceolsige, ship victory.
namesakes: Kelsea Ballerini (country singer of Peter Pan and Half of My Hometown)

assoc.t: Kelsea Ballerini, country-pop singer

e.etymology: The Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Theodore, from Greek Theodoros, theos, god, plus doron, gift.

e.meaning: member of the Gauts, a Germanic tribe
e.etymology: A spelling of Jocelyn, from the Norman name Joscelin, a pet form of a Germanic name based on the tribe of the Gauts or Geats. This spelling is especially popular in Latino families.
The German, Scandinavian and South Slavic spelling of Anya, the Russian pet form of Anna, from Hebrew Hannah, grace or favor.
e.note: Spelled with a J but said AHN-yuh; expect AN-juh from people reading it cold.

e.etymology: The New Testament form of Hebrew Yair (Jair), he gives light. In the Gospels Jairus is the synagogue leader whose young daughter Jesus raises from the dead.
The Italian and Spanish form of Cyrus, from Greek Kyros, the Greek rendering of Old Persian Kurush, the name of the founder of the Persian Empire. It is especially common around Naples.
A J spelling of Giselle, the French form of a Germanic name from gisil, a pledge, as in a noble child raised at another court. The ballet Giselle (1841) spread the name.
From Old Norse sveinn, a boy or young man, later a squire or servant, and the source of English swain. It has been a staple name in Scandinavia for a thousand years.

assoc.t: Sven, Kristoff's reindeer in Disney's Frozen

e.etymology: Coined by Alexandre Dumas for one of the Three Musketeers, after the real musketeer Henri d'Aramitz, whose family took its name from the village of Aramits in the French Pyrenees.
namesakes: Aramis Ramirez (All-Star third baseman for the Chicago Cubs)

assoc.t: Aramis, one of Dumas's Three Musketeers
Aramis, men's cologne from Estée Lauder

e.etymology: The Russian form of Alexander, from Greek Alexandros, alexein, to defend, plus aner, man. Sasha and Sanya are its everyday pet forms.
namesakes: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn (Nobel-winning author of The Gulag Archipelago)

e.etymology: From Persian ravan, soul or spirit, a word also used in Kurdish. The name is widely given to girls across the Arab world, where it is sometimes explained as a river of paradise.
A spelling of Zipporah that follows the Hebrew pronunciation, from tsippor, bird. In Exodus she is the Midianite wife of Moses.
From Arabic layth, one of the classical words for a lion and an image of courage. It is also written Laith.
A romanization of Greek Giannis, the everyday form of Ioannis (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. The spelling Yannis is also popular in France.

assoc.t: NBA star Giannis Antetokounmpo (same sound)

e.etymology: A Welsh name, ar-, an intensifier, plus gwyn, fair or blessed. In Wales it is a men's name with Arwen as the feminine; American parents use it mostly for girls, as a spelling of Arwen, Tolkien's elf princess.

assoc.t: sounds like Arwen, elf princess of The Lord of the Rings

e.meaning: mother whose children are the fish
e.etymology: The Cuban Spanish spelling of Yemoja, the Yoruba orisha of the ocean and motherhood, honored in Santería and Candomblé. The name contracts Yoruba yeye omo eja, mother whose children are fish.

assoc.t: Yemaya, sea goddess of Yoruba religion and Santería

e.etymology: A modern name from Latin America with no traditional meaning, close in sound to Lesly, the Spanish spelling of Leslie, and to Y- names such as Yesenia and Yeslin.

A double-n spelling of Aitana, from the Sierra de Aitana, a mountain range in Alicante, Spain. Poet Rafael Alberti gave the name to his daughter in 1941, and the pop singer Aitana has spread it since 2017.

assoc.t: Aitana, Spanish pop singer

e.etymology: An English place name and surname, from Old English ceorl, a free peasant, and tun, settlement. The hard C, where Charlton has Ch, shows Old Norse influence.
namesakes: Carlton Fisk (Hall of Fame catcher for the Red Sox and White Sox)

assoc.t: Carlton Banks of The Fresh Prince, and his dance

e.etymology: A short form of Victoria for girls and of Victor or Salvatore for boys; Victoria and Victor come from the Latin for victory. Tory is also a surname and the nickname of Britain's Conservative Party.
namesakes: Tory Burch (fashion designer behind the label of the same name)

assoc.t: Tory, a British Conservative; a Loyalist in 1776
Tory Burch, fashion and accessories label

e.etymology: The Late Latin form of John, from Greek Ioannes and Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. It stayed the standard form in German, Dutch and the Nordic languages and gave rise to Johann, Hans and Jan.
namesakes: Johannes Gutenberg (inventor of the movable-type printing press)
Johannes Vermeer (painter of Girl with a Pearl Earring)

e.etymology: An English surname from a place in Kent. American parents first used it in the 1870s for Samuel J. Tilden, who won the popular vote for president in 1876 but lost the disputed election.

assoc.t: Samuel Tilden, loser of the disputed 1876 election

e.etymology: The Arabic and Turkish form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, who is like God? Mikail is one of the archangels named in the Quran.
A modern elaboration of Romeo or Romel with the ending of Carmelo and Angelo, more often spelled Romello. Romeo comes through Italian from a Greek word for a Roman.
A clipped spelling of Cambrie or Cambria. Cambria is the Latin name for Wales, from Welsh Cymry, the Welsh people, literally fellow countrymen.
A Latino elaboration of Briana with the -y ending popular in Dominican and other Caribbean Spanish names. Briana is the feminine of Brian, an Irish name likely from a Celtic root for high or noble.
The English verb bless, from Old English bletsian, to consecrate. It is a modern virtue name in the line of Blessing, used for boys and girls.

assoc.t: bless, the everyday word, as in bless you

e.etymology: A respelling of Marley, an English surname from villages whose names end in Old English leah, a woodland clearing; the first part is variously boundary, marten or pleasant. Bob Marley made the name familiar.

assoc.t: sounds like Marley, as in reggae legend Bob Marley

e.etymology: The English word cloud, from Old English clud, which first meant a rock or hill and was later applied to masses in the sky. It is also a surname, and gamers know it from Cloud Strife of Final Fantasy VII.

assoc.t: cloud, the ordinary word for clouds in the sky
the cloud, internet-based computing and storage
Cloud Strife, hero of Final Fantasy VII

e.etymology: A modern American name with the -iyah ending of Aaliyah. It matches Nazia or Naziya, a Persian and Urdu name from naz, pride, grace or delicacy, though many parents choose it for its sound.
e.note: On paper the name begins with the letters N-a-z-i, which some readers will notice.

e.etymology: Most often the Arabic girls' name Masa, diamond. The same spelling is a Japanese name or short form built on masa, true or elegant, and a South Slavic pet form of Maria written Maša.

assoc.t: masa, the corn dough of tortillas and tamales

e.note: In Spanish, masa is the corn dough used for tortillas and tamales.
